For forty-one years, every street sign in Hollins Ford came from one workshop. Elias Marrow painted them on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring the council at last replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.

What moved the council was a night last winter, when an ambulance crew was called to a house on Upper Gate. The driver mistook Lower Gate for it, as though the two boards had been swapped, and reached the house eleven minutes late. Marrow had given the U and the L the same looping stroke, and under headlights the two names blurred into one shape. The county had issued its rule on reflective letters nine years earlier, and the council filed it away and left every board where it hung.

It was a mix-up that anyone driving the town at night could have seen coming. Half the boards in town were rotting at the edges, and the Gates, among the first Marrow painted, had faded to grey on cream. Dora Pask, the town clerk, had put the county's rule before the council every spring. In the end the council struck a deal with the county for its standard plain letters, made a size larger because the post office asked for larger letters on the new signs. A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.

At a town meeting in June, residents voted to sell the old boards. The few who asked that Marrow's letters be kept on the new signs were outvoted, and after a month in storage at the depot shed the boards went to collectors.

The council should have taken them down the year the county's rule arrived and put up letters that a stranger can read at a glance, instead of waiting for an ambulance to prove the point.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun, and she had built both of them herself long ago. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way. Mrs. Pellow said that depended on how quickly I could count change on a Saturday morning.

Within a month I could lift a frame without flinching. One hot morning in July a swarm boiled out of the nearer hive, rose past the eaves of the shed, and settled in the lilac by the back gate, where I found it humming like a kettle. Mrs. Pellow carried a box out from under the pear tree by her kitchen, gave the branch one firm shake, and had every bee inside before my mother could cross from the clothesline by our back steps.

It was in her workshop that I learned what those hives were. She had cut every joint by hand from cedar, so closely that a knife blade would hardly slip between the pieces, and had sealed each roof seam with pitch she warmed on her stove until it ran like syrup. Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.

In August we took away the full frames, with the sound of the hives carrying in through her kitchen window. On Saturdays I stood at her table at the Brackwell market making change, while she told customers how the boxes were made. She still leaves the hives to look after themselves for a week each August while she visits her daughter in Lisle, and before the first frost she still climbs the ladder onto the shed roof to sweep off the leaves.

Those two hives stand against the fence to this day, and she keeps them still. I have built six hives of my own since, all to her pattern, and the best of them is a shade less square than either of hers.

passage:
Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she began clasping her hands behind her back before every recall. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, sniffed Mara's jacket and told her to leave the liver treats at home. Rook had been coming early for the pocket, not for her.

So for the next two weeks Mara emptied her pockets before every session, and they worked at the empty end of the pitch after Theo's team had gone home. On the first evening Rook broke twice. By the fourth he held every stay, and by the end of the second week he would sit across the grass and wait while Mara counted to sixty.

At the trial, Rook held his sit while the loudspeaker announced the next class, and Mara gave the stay command softly and walked to the far side of the ring. Then, behind the rope, Theo tore open the bag of liver treats he had brought for afterward, and Rook went straight for the sound. The judge scored the recall a zero, and they left without a ribbon. In the parking lot, Theo asked whether they could still stay for the fireworks. "You ripped that bag open right behind the rope, Theo, after I asked you twice to leave it in the car."

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge into a bank of cloud, the streetlights on the hill come on, and still the birds wheel overhead. Then the church clock strikes seven, and the first swifts drop into the chimney; the last children leave the schoolyard and the last bus passes the school gates while the rest pour in after them.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. In 1990 he repointed the whole chimney himself with lime and sand, and he can still tell you which courses of its brick are soft. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds, as he expects it to next year.

The storm two winters ago split the chimney with a crack from its top to the roofline. The council kept the chimney standing, since having it pulled down would have meant scaffolding the whole roof. Reyburn wrote to the council to warn that cement would crack the old brick, and asked for lime, expecting the councillors to agree. They voted for the cheapest bid, and in April a contractor filled the crack with hard grey cement.

The result is a poor repair, a stripe of grey cement from the crack to the chimney's top, so smooth that a swift's claws slide straight off it. The birds keep clear of that stripe and crowd into the old brick below it.

The council should have paid for lime mortar matched to the old brick, which stays rough enough for a swift to grip. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and before they return in May that stripe of cement should be cut out and redone.
